The most famous fish face on the
internet is a museum sculpture,
and the real animal behind it was
stranger than the joke.
Sacabambaspis was a jawless fish
about twenty-five centimeters long,
wrapped in bony armor,
and it swam in Ordovician seas
roughly 450 million years ago,
long before the first dinosaur.
Today we will look at what its
fossils actually say, and why one
disaster may have frozen dozens
of these fish in stone.
Look closely at that famous face.
Two wide, unblinking eyes sit at
the very front of the head,
above a gaping, permanently shocked mouth.
It looks more like a clay project
than a real animal.
The model sits in the Finnish Museum
of Natural History in Helsinki.
In August 2022, a photo of it
spread on Twitter, mostly as a
joke about a badly made reconstruction.
About a year later,
Japanese users found the post and
the fish took off.
They made fan art,
stickers, and plush toys,
and people in Japan fell in love
with its bewildered look.
People could not believe that
something so helpless could have
survived in ancient seas.
So was the model a caricature,
or did the fish really look this ridiculous?
To answer that, we have to go
back to the Ordovician Period,
which lasted from about 485 to
443 million years ago.
This was the age after the Cambrian
Explosion, when animal life had
already spread through the oceans.
The continents looked alien,
with a huge landmass called Gondwana
sitting mostly in the southern hemisphere.
On land there were no trees,
no insects, and no four-legged animals.
Almost all of the drama of life
played out underwater, in warm, shallow seas.
And the face is only the first surprise.
Wait until you see what happened
to dozens of these fish in Bolivia.
The scientific story of
Sacabambaspis starts in the
mountains of Bolivia.
Its fossils come from the Anzaldo
Formation, near the city of Cochabamba.
In 1986, the paleontologists
Pierre-Yves Gagnier, Alain Blieck,
and Gonzalo Rodrigo named the
species Sacabambaspis janvieri.
The genus name combines the nearby
village of Sacabamba with the Greek
word aspis, meaning shield.
The species name honors the French
paleontologist Philippe Janvier,
a leading expert on early fish.
The first description rested on
only a few pieces of armor.
Better specimens came later,
and they showed a whole animal.
When you see an isolated photo
of a fossil or a model,
it is hard to judge size.
Sacabambaspis was small.
An adult was about twenty-five
centimeters long, roughly the length
of a shoe.
Its front half was covered by bony armor.
One large shield covered the back
of the head and body,
and another covered the belly.
Behind that armored front end
trailed a flexible tail,
covered in small scales.
Now the elephant in the room: that face.
In most modern fish,
the eyes sit on the sides of
the head, which gives a wide view
for spotting predators.
Sacabambaspis had its eyes set
toward the front of the head.
The fossils support that part of the model.
Scientists do not agree on exactly
what this layout was for.
One idea is that an animal living
near the sea floor did not need
a wide view.
Whatever the reason, the meme got
the eyes at least partly right.
The most striking feature of
Sacabambaspis is what it did not
have: a jaw.
It belongs to a group called the
jawless fishes.
Instead of upper and lower jaws
that bite, its mouth was a simple
opening, surrounded by small plates.
It could not tear flesh from prey,
and it could not bite to defend itself.
Many scientists think it fed by
taking in small bits of food from
the water or the sea floor,
but we do not have a fossil
of a meal to prove it.
Modern fish and sharks have paired
fins on their sides.
They work like small wings,
helping the fish steer,
roll, and brake.
Sacabambaspis had no paired fins
at all, no pectoral fins and no pelvic fins.
Imagine trying to steer through
open water without rudders.
Sharp turns and hovering in place
would have been very hard for this animal.
So how did it move?
Almost all of its power would have
come from its tail,
which was flattened and ended in a fin.
By swinging its tail from side
to side, it pushed itself forward.
Its head was locked inside a rigid
box of bone, so it could not
bend at the front.
Scientists are still studying
exactly how well it swam.
Its armor was not only a shield,
it also held a sensing system.
Under a microscope, the surface
of the armor shows grooves and pits.
In early fishes like this one,
such grooves held a sense organ,
called the lateral line,
that picks up vibrations in the water.
If that was true for Sacabambaspis,
its skin worked a bit like a
motion detector, and it could feel
a predator moving nearby even
without sharp eyesight.
Why did early fish put so much
energy into heavy armor instead of speed?
The armor was made of a very
old kind of bone tissue called aspidin.
It had layers, like a sandwich.
A thin layer lay at the base,
a spongy layer sat in the middle,
and a hard, ridged layer sat on top.
We do not know for sure what
attacked these fish.
One idea is that large predators
of the time, such as big sea
scorpions called eurypterids and
shelled cephalopods, made armor worth having.
To see where this strange design
came from, rewind another fifty
million years or so,
to the Cambrian Period.
In the Chengjiang fossil beds of
China, paleontologists found
Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia,
tiny, finger-sized animals with
eyes and a flexible rod along the back.
They are among the earliest known vertebrates.
They had no bony armor at all.
For tens of millions of years,
vertebrates stayed soft.
Then armor appeared, and animals
like Sacabambaspis were wearing it.
That change happened in a world
with new kinds of large hunters,
and a hard shell suddenly paid off.
Armor tells us something odd about
our own bones.
We think of bone as something deep
inside us, hidden under muscle and skin.
But in the fossil record,
some of the earliest bone we find
in vertebrates is armor on the
outside of the body,
like the shields of Sacabambaspis.
A popular idea is that bone started
outside the body and later moved
inward to become the skeleton.
That idea is still debated,
but these armored fishes are central
to the argument.
Think about how odd that is.
The first thing many vertebrates
built out of minerals was not a
skeleton to hold up a body.
It was a coat.
A fish that could not bite back
could still make itself hard to bite.
Now back to the Helsinki model.
Why does it look so shocked?
The honest answer is that nobody
built it to be funny.
Reconstructing a fish from
flattened, broken fossils is hard,
and a sculptor has to decide what
the soft parts looked like.
Different choices give different
faces, and the model's wide-open
mouth is one such choice.
Scientists today usually draw
Sacabambaspis with a more
streamlined head and a smaller mouth opening.
The meme face is one artist's guess,
not a photograph of the past.
The Bolivian fossil site also holds a puzzle.
Sacabambaspis fossils are often
found in groups.
In one area, about thirty specimens
were packed into a very small space,
many of them articulated,
which means their bones were still
lying together.
Living fish do not die in neat
piles like that, so something
unusual happened.
A study published in 2007,
led by Davies, looked at the rocks
and the fossils and proposed an explanation.
The fish and a group of shelled
animals called brachiopods were
probably killed by floods of fresh
water and surges of mud,
which buried them quickly in shallow
water near the coast.
Sudden burial is the key.
It protected the bodies from
scavengers and decay, and that
is how a fragile fish became a fossil.
Some writers suggest a big storm
was the trigger.
That part is likely,
but it is still an interpretation,
not a proven fact.
Why did the jawless fish not rule
the seas forever?
Without jaws, they could not bite,
grab, or chew.
Then something changed.
Scientists think that parts of
the gill supports, the bones that
hold up the gills,
were reshaped into hinged jaws.
That event gave rise to the jawed
vertebrates, which include sharks,
bony fish, and us.
With jaws, an animal could attack
large prey, and the oceans changed.
By the Devonian Period,
more than sixty million years after
Sacabambaspis, armored jawed fish
called placoderms ruled the seas.
The most famous, Dunkleosteus,
had bony plates in its mouth that
worked like blades.
For years, people said it grew
to nine meters or more.
A 2023 study suggests a typical
adult was only about three and
a half meters long,
and the largest known one about four.
Still a very dangerous animal.
Sacabambaspis itself was long gone by then.
But in a world of fast jawed
hunters, slow, finless fishes became
less and less common.
Sacabambaspis lived at a dangerous time.
About 444 million years ago,
near the end of the Ordovician,
Earth entered a brief,
deep ice age.
Glaciers grew over Gondwana,
and sea levels dropped.
The shallow seas where many animals
lived shrank away.
The cold, and low oxygen in parts
of the deep ocean,
helped cause one of the biggest
mass extinctions in Earth's history.
Roughly eighty-five percent of
marine species disappeared.
We do not know exactly when the
last Sacabambaspis died.
We know that the world it lived
in came to an end.
Did any jawless fish make it to
the present day?
Yes, but not armored ones.
Lampreys and hagfish are the only
living jawless fish.
They have slimy, soft,
eel-like bodies, and no bony armor.
Some scientists think their
ancestors lost armor along the
way, while others think they never had it.
They are not descendants of Sacabambaspis.
They are distant cousins that show
what a body without jaws looks like today.
A lamprey has a round,
toothed suction mouth that latches
onto its prey.
Sacabambaspis was not our great-grandparent.
It was more like a distant cousin,
a member of a side branch of
the family tree of vertebrates.
Still, animals like it help us
understand how our own body plan
came together, including bone,
a head with sense organs,
and a protective skin.
These traits did not appear all at once.
They were built, piece by piece,
over tens of millions of years.
That is why evolution is not a
ladder that climbs toward a perfect animal.
It is a branching bush full of
strange experiments, dead ends, and survivors.
Sacabambaspis was one of those
experiments, and for millions of
years it worked very well.
It was small, armored,
and a little odd.
So the next time that meme scrolls
past your screen, pause for a second
before you laugh.
The face is a guess by an artist.
But the fish was real,
and so was its world.
It was a small,
armored animal that felt the water
with its skin, lived without jaws
or paired fins, and left a snapshot
of life that we can still read in stone.
